analysis.title: Global Rates Notes: 4Q26 Treasury Refunding Preview
key_insights: GS expects Treasury to lower near-term borrowing projections at its 3pm Monday, November 2 financing release, estimating 4Q26 marketable borrowing of $571bn, including $286bn of net bills, versus $628bn projected at the August refunding.
The lower borrowing estimate partly reflects a higher starting TGA balance than Treasury projected previously. GS assumes a $850bn end-of-Q4 cash balance.
GS estimates 1Q27 marketable borrowing of $713bn, assuming a $900bn end-of-quarter cash balance target.
GS economists project deficits of $2.0tn/$2.1tn/$2.1tn for FY27/28/29, modestly below their previous baseline, reflecting larger than expected corporate tax receipts.
Base case: Treasury maintains or modestly increases buyback envelope sizes, keeps 10-to-30y auction sizes steady, and begins increasing 2-to-7y auction sizes in May 2027.

Risk case: Treasury cuts long-end auction sizes after the August guidance tweak ('changes' rather than 'increases') and the mid-August buyback upsizing. GS says this is not its base case. The surprise buyback increase also makes it hard to strictly rule out eliminating the 20y point.

GS gives four reasons for steady 10-to-30y sizes: fiscal needs favor a flexible array of liquid benchmarks, there is limited room to cut 20y sizes before liquidity suffers, the prior guidance of unchanged sizes for 'at least the next several quarters' makes a change counter to predictability, and there is little sign of long-end indigestion attributable to supply.

GS views buybacks as a more flexible tool for managing the maturity composition of debt. Stating explicitly that buybacks are part of that toolkit, rather than only for 'liquidity support', could strengthen market impact if Treasury becomes less price sensitive in operations.
GS thinks the larger long-end buybacks have compressed long-end dispersion and supported spreads. Swap spread widening since the buyback upsizing was most pronounced at points that started tighter.

GS expects further refunding guidance changes that nod to possible auction size adjustments, with two-sided wording. One example is 'Treasury anticipates it may be appropriate to consider changes to nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes over the next several quarters.'

Demand trends: less price sensitive non-Fed buyers keep a diminished footprint, foreign official buyers are unlikely to add net demand without material dollar weakness, and defined benefit pension demand has shrunk, leaving long-term saver demand closer to the Aggregate Bond Index maturity mix.

GS argues for a more front-end and belly-focused supply mix, with continued meaningful reliance on T-bills. It expects the Fed to keep adding Treasuries through bill purchases until it reaches a market-consistent share, which GS estimates happens in 2028, and sees this as somewhat vol dampening.
GS projects unchanged coupon auction sizes through 1Q27, then gradual increases limited to 2-to-7y maturities (for example the 2y rising from $69bn in Oct-26 to $71bn in May-27 and $87bn by 2028).

Treasury could take the more dramatic step of eliminating the 20y point, which GS cannot strictly rule out.
Foreign official demand is unlikely to rebuild without material dollar weakness.

charts_described: Exhibit 2 plots the change in SOFR swap spreads since August 18 against starting spread levels, with widening most pronounced at points that started tighter.
Exhibit 5 projects monthly coupon auction sizes through Dec-28, with unchanged sizes through 1Q27 and gradual increases limited to 2-to-7y maturities afterward.
vol_and_positioning: GS expects Fed Treasury purchases through bills to be somewhat vol dampening, with the pace depending on funding conditions.
Leaning on front-end and intermediate coupon supply could reduce interest expense volatility and lower the risk of supply imbalances worsening rate volatility at particular curve points.

tension_points.bull_case: GS base case is that Treasury keeps 10-to-30y auction sizes steady and relies on buybacks and 2-to-7y increases from May 2027, because fiscal needs favor flexible liquid benchmarks and there is little sign of supply-driven indigestion.
tension_points.bear_case: Treasury could cut long-end auction sizes after the August guidance tweak and larger buybacks, and a move to eliminate the 20y point cannot be strictly ruled out.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A change in refunding guidance language or an announced cut to long-end auction sizes at the November 2 release would contradict the steady-size base case.

theme_stances.key_argument: Treasury likely keeps 10-to-30y sizes steady, uses buybacks for maturity management, and starts raising 2-to-7y sizes in May 2027.
Demand trends support continued meaningful use of T-bills and more front-end and belly coupon supply.
theme_stances.evidence: room for Treasury to continue relying meaningfully on T-bills
